llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Education and Adult Mortality in the United States, Cohorts 1908-1939”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) IV combined with a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences/event-study framework.

•  First stage (relevance): Exploit cross-state, cross-cohort changes in compulsory-schooling laws (CSLs) to instrument for completed years of schooling.  
•  Second stage (causal effect): Estimate the impact of an additional year of schooling on the probability of dying in a given follow-up window (or on an indicator for death by some cutoff age).

Why IV + DID/Event Study is appropriate  
– Years of schooling are chosen; simple OLS is confounded by ability, family background, health endowments, etc.  
– CSLs shifted schooling exogenously across birth cohorts within states and at different times, giving a natural experiment.  
– With state-of-birth and cohort fixed effects (and their interaction, if preferred), identification comes from within-state, within-cohort changes induced by law revisions, mimicking a difference-in-differences. The event-study version lets us test for pre-trends.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
  Edu_i  = completed years of schooling for individual i.

Instrument(s):  
  CSL_{st}  = minimum years of schooling mandated in state s for a child born in year t.  
  Alt: PostLaw_{st} = 1 if year-of-birth cohort t in state s faced a higher compulsory minimum than the cohort born t-1.

Control/Counterfactual:  
  Individuals in the same state born immediately before the CSL change (and all cohorts in states where the CSL did not change) serve as the counterfactual.

Timing:  
  An individual is “exposed” if her age of required schooling or required leaving age increased before she turned 14 (standard assumption in CSL literature). Exact event date = year the law became effective; birth cohorts 0–2 years after the law change are treated, −5 to −1 serve as pre-trend.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance: CSL changes shifted educational attainment.  
     Plausible and testable in first stage.

A2. Exclusion restriction: CSL affects adult mortality only through its impact on education.  
     Plausible given schooling is the main channel, but need to rule out confounders (e.g., CSLs also curtailed child labor → income).

A3. No differential migration correlated with CSL: Families did not move across state lines in response to CSLs in a way correlated with later mortality.  
     Historically limited, but we can test with birthplace vs. state of residence.

A4. Cohort-by-state trends: In absence of the law, mortality trends would have evolved similarly across treated and control cohorts within a state.  
     Checked with event-study pre-coefficients.

A5. Monotonicity/SUTVA for IV: CSLs weakly increase (never decrease) schooling; no spillovers across individuals.  
     Reasonable—laws raise the minimum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Simultaneous child-labor or public-health legislation.  
    – Control for state-year covariates: child-labor laws, GDP per capita, public-health spending, wartime mobilization dummies.  
    – Include state-specific linear (or higher-order) cohort trends.

T2. Selective migration or mortality selection before observation.  
    – Restrict to state of birth × birth cohort cells; re-estimate on sub-sample that never moved (if place-of-residence available).  
    – Use information on age at death vs. attrition to test for selective survival.

T3. Measurement error in schooling or incorrect exposure window.  
    – Robustness to alternative exposure definitions (birth year vs. age 6 start year).  
    – Use grouped-cohort (state × 5-year cohort) aggregation, which attenuates individual misreporting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE and IV
library(did)         # event-study pre-trend check
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("nlms_census_csl_1908_1939.csv")   # one row per individual

# 2. Variable construction -----------------------------------------
dt[, birth_cohort := year_of_birth]
dt[, treated := ifelse(birth_cohort >= law_effective_year, 1, 0), by = state_birth]

# Compulsory minimum years of schooling the cohort faced
dt[, csl_years := min_years_required]

# Main outcome: died by age 60 indicator (example)
dt[, died60 := as.integer(age_at_death <= 60)]

# Exposure window alternative (robustness)
dt[, treated_alt := ifelse(birth_cohort >= (law_effective_year - 1), 1, 0), by = state_birth]

# 3. 2SLS main specification ---------------------------------------
# FE: state of birth, year of birth, race × gender, plus controls
est_iv <- feols(died60 ~ 1 | 0 | 
                  iv(Edu ~ csl_years) | 
                  state_birth + birth_cohort + race + gender,
                data = dt, cluster = ~state_birth)

summary(est_iv)

# First stage for relevance
fs <- feols(Edu ~ csl_years | state_birth + birth_cohort + race + gender,
            data = dt, cluster = ~state_birth)
summary(fs)

# 4. Event-study (pre-trend) check ---------------------------------
# relative cohort to law change
dt[, rel_cohort := birth_cohort - law_effective_year]

# Keep −10 to +10
dt_es <- dt[rel_cohort >= -10 & rel_cohort <= 10]

es <- feols(died60 ~ i(rel_cohort, ref = -1) | state_birth + birth_cohort + race + gender,
            data = dt_es, cluster = ~state_birth)

iplot(es) + theme_minimal()

# 5. Robustness: alternate outcome and controls --------------------
# Re-estimate using age-standardized mortality hazard
est_iv2 <- feols(mortality_hazard ~ 1 | 0 | iv(Edu ~ csl_years) |
                   state_birth + birth_cohort + state_trend,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state_birth)
summary(est_iv2)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory and prior evidence (Grossman 1972; Lleras-Muney 2005) predict higher education lowers mortality through better health behaviors, access to information, and earnings.  
• Sign: negative effect—each additional year of schooling reduces the probability of dying before age 60.  
• Magnitude (rough prior): 1 extra year ↓ mortality rate by about 1–2 deaths per 1,000 person-years (≈ a 2–4 % relative decline for these cohorts).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV strategy)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) ............... 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction (no other channel) ......... 0.5  
C3: No selective migration/endogenous sample ......... 0.5  
C4: Stable unit treatment / no spillovers ............ 1  
C5: Monotonicity (no defiers) ........................ 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → generally credible but exclusion & migration warrant careful robustness work.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
END
